message.content:
**Answer**

The last common ancestor of a lion (*Panthera leo*) and a zebra (*Equus quagga*) is the last common ancestor of all placental mammals (Eutheria). In other words, the two species share a common ancestor that lived before the split between the two major mammalian clades that gave rise to modern carnivores (Carnivora) and odd‑toed ungulates (Perissodactyla).

**Key points**

| Group | Taxonomic rank | Relationship to lion & zebra | Approximate age of last common ancestor |
|-------|----------------|-----------------------------|----------------------------------------|
| **Felidae** | Family | Lion’s family | ~10–15 Mya (within Carnivora) |
| **Equidae** | Family | Zebra’s family | ~5–10 Mya (within Perissodactyla) |
| **Carnivora** | Order | Lion’s order | ~20–30 Mya |
| **Perissodactyla** | Order | Zebra’s order | ~20–30 Mya |
| **Eutheria** | Clade (placental mammals) | Last common ancestor of lion & zebra | ~160 Mya |

- The divergence between the lineages that led to Carnivora (including lions) and Perissodactyla (including zebras) occurred roughly 100–120 million years ago.
- The deeper split that separates placental mammals from marsupials and monotremes happened around 160–170 million years ago.

So, while lions and zebras share a relatively recent common ancestor within their own families, their most recent common ancestor that is shared by both species is the ancestor of all placental mammals, dating back to the late Jurassic/early Cretaceous period.
